title: Privilege Escalation via Unvalidated Farm Member Scopes
description: The UpdateFarmMemberDto accepts an arbitrary string array for `scopes` (line 19) with no validation against known FARM_SCOPE values. The FarmMembersService.update() method passes these scopes directly to Prisma (line 81) without checking if they are valid scope strings. A member with `invitations.manage` permission can set scopes to `["*"]` (the wildcard scope), granting themselves owner-equivalent access to the entire farm — including finance, health records, livestock management, and marketplace operations. The service blocks assigning `MembershipRole.owner` role (line 66-69) but does not prevent granting the wildcard scope that provides the same privileges. Additionally, no check prevents a member from updating their own membership record (the guard only blocks modifying the farm owner), enabling self-escalation.
impact: Any farm collaborator with `invitations.manage` scope can escalate to full owner-level permissions on the farm, gaining unrestricted access to financial data, livestock records, health records, marketplace operations, and the ability to grant the same privileges to others.
attack_path:
1. Attacker has a farm membership with `invitations.manage` scope.
2. Attacker sends PATCH /farms/:farmId/members/:ownMembershipId with body {"scopes": ["*"]}.
3. The service validates the actor has `invitations.manage` scope (passes), checks the target is not the owner (passes for non-owner members), and directly writes ["*"] to the membership scopes.
4. On subsequent requests, getEffectiveFarmScopes() returns Set(["*"]) and scopeSatisfies() returns true for any required scope check.
5. Attacker now has full farm access equivalent to the owner.
evidence: UpdateFarmMemberDto.scopes is typed as `string[]` with only @IsString({each:true}) and @ArrayMaxSize(50) validators (update-farm-member.dto.ts:15-19). No @IsIn() or @IsEnum() decorator restricts values to valid FARM_SCOPE entries. farm-members.service.ts:80-81 writes dto.scopes directly: `...(dto.scopes !== undefined ? { scopes: dto.scopes } : {})`. The wildcard scope "*" is checked at farm-access.service.ts:65: `if (effective.has(FARM_SCOPE.ALL)) { return true; }` where FARM_SCOPE.ALL = "*" (farm-scopes.constants.ts:3).
remediation: Add an @IsIn() validator on UpdateFarmMemberDto.scopes to restrict values to the known FARM_SCOPE entries (excluding the wildcard "*"). In the service, reject any scope value that equals "*" or matches a wildcard pattern. Also add a check to prevent a member from modifying their own membership: `if (row.userId === actor.id) throw new ForbiddenException('Cannot modify own permissions')`. Apply the same fix to CreateFarmInvitationDto.scopes.

title: Buyer Email Addresses Exposed to Sellers via Marketplace Offers
description: Three code paths in the marketplace module expose buyer email addresses to sellers who should only see display names: (1) OffersService.listReceived() at line 321 includes `buyer: { select: { id: true, fullName: true, email: true } }` in the Prisma query, returning buyer emails to the seller for all received offers. (2) OffersService.accept() at line 460 returns all offers with buyer emails after accepting an offer. (3) ListingsService.getById() at line 881 returns all offers with buyer emails when the seller views their own listing. While the listing's seller info is properly sanitized via sanitizeSellerForViewer() (which strips email for non-owner viewers), no equivalent sanitization exists for buyer data in these offer-related queries.
impact: Sellers can harvest email addresses of all buyers who submit offers on their listings. This exposes buyer PII across trust boundaries, potentially enabling unsolicited contact, phishing, or data aggregation. In a marketplace with many active buyers, this could expose hundreds of email addresses per seller.
attack_path:
1. Seller publishes a listing on the marketplace.
2. Multiple buyers submit offers on the listing.
3. Seller calls GET /marketplace/offers/received.
4. Response includes `buyer.email` for every offer, exposing all buyers' email addresses.
5. Alternatively, seller views their listing via GET /marketplace/listings/:id and receives all offers with buyer emails in the `offers` array.
evidence: offers.service.ts:321 — `buyer: { select: { id: true, fullName: true, email: true } }` in listReceived(). offers.service.ts:460 — same pattern in accept(). listings.service.ts:881 — same pattern in getById() seller path. Compare with the seller info in listings.service.ts:910-922 where sanitizeSellerForViewer() properly strips email for non-owners.
remediation: Remove `email: true` from the buyer select clauses in all three locations. If the seller needs to contact the buyer, use the in-app chat system that already exists (ChatService is used elsewhere in OffersService). Alternatively, only expose buyer email after a transaction reaches a specific status (e.g. payment confirmed), not for all pending offers.

title: Farm Member List and Update Responses Expose User Email and Phone
description: The FarmMembersService.list() method (line 28-41) returns all farm members with their email and phone: `user: { select: { id: true, fullName: true, email: true, phone: true } }`. Similarly, the update() method (line 82-88) returns the updated member with the same fields. Any farm member with `chat` scope (the minimum required to call list()) can see emails and phone numbers of all other farm members. While some information sharing among farm collaborators may be expected, exposing raw PII (especially phone numbers) to any member with the most basic scope creates unnecessary data exposure.
impact: Any farm collaborator with the minimal `chat` scope can enumerate emails and phone numbers of all other farm members. This PII could be misused for spam, social engineering, or exfiltrated if the member's account is compromised.
attack_path:
1. Attacker obtains a farm membership with `chat` scope (the minimum scope).
2. Attacker calls GET /farms/:farmId/members.
3. Response includes `user.email` and `user.phone` for every farm member.
4. Attacker collects PII of all farm members.
evidence: farm-members.service.ts:32-38 — `user: { select: { id: true, fullName: true, email: true, phone: true } }` in list(). farm-members.service.ts:83-86 — same select in update(). The list endpoint only requires FARM_SCOPE.chat (farm-members.controller.ts:26).
remediation: Remove `email` and `phone` from the user select in list() and update() responses. If collaborators need to contact each other, the in-app chat system should be used instead. Alternatively, only expose these fields to members with `invitations.manage` scope.

title: Seller Full Name Exposed to All Authenticated Users in Marketplace Listings
description: In the public listing feed (ListingsService.list(), non-mine path, line 519), the seller's full name is included via `seller: { select: { id: true, fullName: true } }`. While the detail endpoint (getById) properly uses privacyDisplayName() to show only the first name and last initial, the public list endpoint exposes the seller's complete full name to every authenticated user. This is inconsistent with the privacy model established by the privacyDisplayName() function and the sanitizeSellerForViewer() method.
impact: Every authenticated user can see sellers' complete full names when browsing the marketplace feed, enabling identification and profiling of sellers. Combined with farm name and location label, this could allow real-world identification of livestock producers.
attack_path:
1. Any authenticated user calls GET /marketplace/listings.
2. Response includes `seller.fullName` (complete name) for every published listing.
3. User can enumerate and identify all active sellers on the platform.
evidence: listings.service.ts:518-520 — `seller: { select: { id: true, fullName: true } }` returns full names in list feed. Compare with listings.service.ts:89-100 where privacyDisplayName() truncates to 'FirstName L.' format, and listings.service.ts:910-922 where sanitizeSellerForViewer() uses the same logic.
remediation: Apply privacyDisplayName() to the seller data in the public listing feed, consistent with how it's used in getById(). Rename the seller.fullName field to sellerDisplayName in the feed response to make the privacy transformation explicit.

title: Unauthenticated Fee Quote Endpoint Enables Information Disclosure
description: The WalletController.feeQuote() endpoint (GET /users/me/wallet/fee-quote, line 59-62) does not use @CurrentUser() and the query parameters go directly to the fee calculation service without any user context. While the controller class has @UseGuards(SupabaseJwtGuard), making it technically authenticated, the endpoint itself does not use the authenticated user context. More critically, there is no rate limit override on this endpoint (unlike the financial transaction endpoints which have @Throttle decorators). This allows rapid enumeration of the fee structure for all transaction types and amounts.
impact: An authenticated user can rapidly enumerate the complete fee schedule (all transaction types and amounts) without rate limiting, potentially revealing business-sensitive pricing information or fee tier breakpoints that should only be visible in context of actual transactions.
attack_path:
1. Authenticated user calls GET /users/me/wallet/fee-quote?type=<type>&amount=<amount> with varying parameters.
2. Without per-endpoint rate limiting (only the global 200/min applies), the user can rapidly enumerate fees for all WalletFeeTransactionType values and amount ranges.
3. Complete fee structure is disclosed.
evidence: wallet.controller.ts:59-62 — feeQuote() has no @Throttle() decorator unlike top-up, withdraw, and transfer endpoints which all have @Throttle({ default: { limit: 3, ttl: 60_000 } }) or @Throttle({ default: { limit: 5, ttl: 60_000 } }).
remediation: Add a @Throttle() decorator to the feeQuote() endpoint consistent with other wallet endpoints. Consider whether the fee structure should be publicly queryable or only returned in the context of initiating a specific transaction.

title: Platform Feature Flags Endpoint Skips Rate Limiting and Authentication
description: The PlatformFeatureFlagsController applies @SkipThrottle() at the class level (line 23) and has no authentication guard on the GET /platform/feature-flags and GET /platform/feature-flags/:moduleId endpoints (only the POST notify-me endpoint has @UseGuards(SupabaseJwtGuard)). This means these endpoints are completely unauthenticated AND exempt from rate limiting. While the data returned (module enabled/disabled status) may be intended to be public, the combination of no auth and no rate limiting makes this an enumeration target.
impact: Unauthenticated and unlimited access allows reconnaissance of all platform module states (which features are enabled, disabled, or in maintenance). An attacker can monitor feature flag changes in real-time without any rate limiting, potentially timing attacks around feature deployments or outages.
attack_path:
1. Attacker calls GET /api/v1/platform/feature-flags repeatedly without authentication.
2. @SkipThrottle() ensures no rate limiting is applied.
3. Attacker enumerates all module IDs and their states.
4. By polling continuously, attacker can detect configuration changes in real-time.
evidence: platform-feature-flags.controller.ts:23 — @SkipThrottle() on the class. platform-feature-flags.controller.ts:28-31 — list() has no @UseGuards. Only notifyMe() at line 47 has @UseGuards(SupabaseJwtGuard).
remediation: Remove @SkipThrottle() from the class level. Apply a moderate rate limit to the public endpoints. If these endpoints must be public for mobile app bootstrapping, consider applying a separate restrictive rate limit like @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } }).

title: Farm Invitation DTO Allows Arbitrary Scopes Including Wildcard
description: The CreateFarmInvitationDto.scopes field (line 51-54) accepts an arbitrary string array with no validation against known FARM_SCOPE values, mirroring the same vulnerability as UpdateFarmMemberDto. A user with invitation management permissions can create invitations that grant the wildcard scope ["*"] to new members, giving them owner-equivalent permissions upon joining.
impact: A farm collaborator with invitation management permissions can create invitations that grant full farm access to any new member, bypassing the intended role-based access control system.
attack_path:
1. Attacker with `invitations.manage` scope creates a farm invitation with body containing `{"scopes": ["*"]}`.
2. The invited user joins the farm and receives wildcard scope permissions.
3. The new member has full access equivalent to the farm owner.
evidence: create-farm-invitation.dto.ts:51-54 — `scopes` field uses @IsArray(), @IsString({each:true}), @ArrayMaxSize(50) but no @IsIn() or scope validation. Same pattern as update-farm-member.dto.ts.
remediation: Add an @IsIn() validator restricting values to the known FARM_SCOPE entries (excluding the wildcard "*"). Reject wildcard scopes in the invitation creation service.
